facts.claim: Google’s SRE Workbook defines canarying as trying a change on part of a service for a limited time and judging it: the part that gets the change is the canary, the rest is the control.
The SRE Workbook’s worked example uses a canary of 5% of traffic: a change that fails 20% of its requests there fails only 1% of all requests.
The same chapter calls canarying effectively an A/B test: if the canary’s share of errors is close to the control’s, the deployment goes on.
It warns that a check that is overly strict gives lots of false alarms, and that a canary should last long enough to stand for the whole deployment.
For a bad canary, it says to pause and roll back the deployment, or call a person to help.

CrowdStrike says its 19 July 2024 update went out at 04:09 UTC to Windows machines running its security software (version 7.11 or later) that were online, and was pulled back 78 minutes later, at 05:27 UTC.
CrowdStrike’s root cause analysis (August 2024) says all 12 of its automated test cases put a match-anything value in the field that later crashed machines, so the tests never met the bug.
The same analysis says each such update should have gone out in a staged rollout: a canary first, then wider and wider groups, or rolled back if problems show.
Pete Hodgson (martinfowler.com, 2017) describes feature toggles as patterns for delivering new features rapidly but safely, separating a feature’s release from the code’s deployment.
LaunchDarkly, a feature flag service, says changes made in its dashboard typically reach the apps using it within 200 milliseconds (vendor-reported, checked 2026-10-30).
Danilo Sato (martinfowler.com, 2014) describes parallel change for changes the old version can’t work with: expand to support old and new, move every user over, then contract to remove the old.

DORA (checked 2026-10-30) measures software delivery with five numbers: how long a change takes to ship, how often teams deploy, how often a deploy fails, how long recovery from a failed deploy takes, and how often unplanned deploys follow an incident.
facts.value: change lead time, deployment frequency, change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time, deployment rework rate

facts.claim: DORA defines failed deployment recovery time as how long it takes to recover from a deploy that fails and needs someone to step in at once.
